title: ‘I’ve been good in 2026, but I prefer to be outstanding at least one or two days a year’: Michael Storer Q&A
content:
Cyclist
‘I’ve been good in 2026, but I prefer to be outstanding at least one or two days a year’: Michael Storer Q&A

Can you remember the first bike race you won and how?

Not the very first, but one of the first was this really hilly club race in a town called Brigadoon in Australia. I was 12 and it was probably one of the hardest loops you could make in Perth, with these steep ramps with 20% gradients up and downhill. It was maybe only 30 or 40km long, but it was a pure climber’s course and I won it solo. I did appreciate the $30 bike voucher that they gave us as a prize in those days too. You could get quite a lot with that: a couple of spare tubes, a new bike light or maybe some other accessories.

There are a number of pro cyclists who come from Perth; there’s you, Jai Hindley, Ben O’Connor…

Luke Durbridge, Cam Meyer…

What’s in the water? What has made it such a hotspot for cyclists?

It was mostly thanks to Jai’s dad [Gordon]. He was just one of the coaches there who influenced Midland Cycle Club and pushed it in a direction that was better for high performance. He had some contagious enthusiasm, he was really good at getting a lot more kids involved and he knew a thing or two about pro cycling as well. That made a big difference to the club’s general culture.

You were studying a chemistry degree at university and considering doing that over pro cycling. What changed your mind?

It was more splitting the approach, not putting all my eggs in one basket. I still had some belief in pro cycling, of course, but I was keeping the studying alive just in case. I also switched to psychology for the last year, but I stopped studying when I signed my pro contract [in 2017] – until then, you never know. If you really want to maximise being a pro cyclist, I think it’s almost better if you don’t study. It comes with risk of burnout as well.

While your breakthrough came at the 2021 Vuelta with two stage wins, it seems like joining Tudor Pro Cycling in 2024 coincided with a rise in your consistency and performance. What changed?

After what was kind of two lost years at Groupama-FDJ [in 2022 and 2023], I was restarting where I left off. I still won the Tour de l’Ain [in 2023], so it wasn’t all bad, but I didn’t progress that extra bit. Groupama didn’t have the support to bring me to a higher level. At Tudor I have that support to find that extra bit of improvement, which can really make a difference in results.

They just work on everything. It can be something as basic as bike positioning, both on the time-trial and road bike, which is super-important. There’s better coaching, and the team culture has a big influence. I feel a lot more motivated to do well in this team and it makes a difference if you feel good, then you have more of a positive mindset to impact your form. At previous teams it maybe wasn’t the best environment and I’d be looking forward to going home each time after a race.

You’re more of a climber than anything else. Do you think climbers have a different personality type to sprinters?

With the nature of sprinting, you have to be a bit more assertive, borderline aggressive; in climbing, you don’t necessarily need those characteristics to be successful.

You’ve lived mainly in Italy and San Marino since 2016. Have you picked up any Italian traits?

Probably being critical over food; no cappuccino past 12 o’clock; no undercooked or over-cooked pasta. Also, I hate it if the sauce is undercooked and watery.

What are your thoughts about pineapple on pizza?

Definitely not.

Your diet is plant-based. Have you noticed gains in terms of performance or feeling?

That’s the right way to describe it – plant-based, not plant-exclusive – I’ve had one steak this year because I like it once a year, a little treat at a training camp. The main benefit initially was just better knowledge of nutrition. I haven’t done a PubMed [database of health articles] search and there isn’t much research on vegan diet and performance yet the consensus is there’s no impact, which is good. If there’s no negatives and positive other things, then why not?

You finished third at Il Lombardia in 2025 to Tadej Pogačar. What was that experience like, going toe-to-toe with the dominant force in cycling?

Surreal. I was confident of a top ten, which was the goal, and I remember feeling good on the second-to-last climb. I was counting the number of guys left in the group, which also gives motivation. Then I heard on the radio about some strong riders getting dropped, including Del Toro and Seixas. So at least if he [Seixas] is the next Pogačar, I can say I beat him once.

That day I went super-deep. I could hardly stand up at the finish line. I could feel muscle failure, it hurt just walking up and down the podium steps; proper pain. That’s when you know you’ve gone extremely deep.

Did Pogačar at least look drained?

No, the usual jumping around, smiling – I was smiling too, but couldn’t jump anymore. He said, ‘Well done.’ I think he was a little bit surprised to see me on the podium.

Has that helped your confidence?

Even if it happens once a season, if I have that one day where I’m flying and get a top result, that’s super-exciting. I hope to get the ball rolling a bit more. I’ve been thereabouts in 2026, I’ve been good, but I prefer to be outstanding at least one or two days a year.
